area.howPriority: How the priority score is made
area.howPriorityBody: Each part is turned into a percentile within the reach, then weighted:
area.formulaSection: section = {{risk}} × model rank + {{retreat}} × recent retreat + {{pop}} × people + {{bldg}} × buildings
area.howPriorityFoot: The weights are design choices, not measured contributions. They should be agreed with local officials before any real use.
area.exposureBody: Population is the WorldPop {{year}} estimate; buildings are from Google Open Buildings v3 (confidence ≥ 0.75). Both describe who lives near the bank today. Neither is a count of people or houses that will be lost.

river.aboutTitle: What these lines and patches are
river.aboutBankline: A bankline is the edge of the land along the main channel, traced from Sentinel-1 radar composites of one dry season (November to April), when the river is low and the edge is stable.
river.aboutErosion: Erosion for a monsoon is land in one dry season that is river or sand in the next. Patches smaller than 1 ha, or not touching the main channel, are removed as noise.
river.aboutSum: Adding the yearly bars gives the sum of annual mapped erosion, not the unique land lost: a char can be lost, rebuilt and lost again.
river.mapLabel: Map of banklines and erosion in the {{region}}

nisar.title: Land-to-water change seen by NISAR, 2026
nisar.explain: The map shows land from the 2026 dry-season map that was open water in each of the last two passes up to {{date}}. The river is still high in September, so part of this is flooding, not lost land.
nisar.chartTitle: Water in the reach at each pass
nisar.chartAria: Lines: hectares of open water and of flooded dry-season land at each NISAR pass
nisar.checkTitle: Did High sections see major change so far?
nisar.checkIntro: Share of sections in this reach with at least {{ha}} ha of NISAR change, counted the same way as the model's training target.
nisar.checkCaption: Provisional. Erosion before 18 June and on the falling river (October–November) is not yet included.
nisar.noFrames: Radar image playback is not available: the image frames are not part of this snapshot. The chart above uses the actual pass dates.
nisar.aboutBody: NISAR is the NASA–ISRO L-band radar mission. These are provisional GCOV products (track 69, frame 14), put on the same 20 m grid as the 2026 Sentinel-1 land map. A pixel counts as changed only if it is open water in each of the two latest passes and within 1 km of the dry-season river.
nisar.aboutMetrics: Model-versus-baseline scores for this check (top 20% flagged per reach) are on the How it works page. They use a different cut from the map's High class (top 10%).

how.title: How <hl>it works</hl>
how.lede: From satellite radar to a ranking of riverbank sections, and how well that ranking held up on years it had not seen.

process.title: From radar to a ranking
process.body: Clouds hide the Jamuna for most of the monsoon, so the system uses radar, which sees through them. Every step below runs offline in Python; this site shows a fixed, checked snapshot of the results.

radar.title: Radar each dry season
radar.body: A median of Sentinel-1 images for each dry season, November to April, 2015–2026. Smooth water returns little signal and looks dark; land looks bright.

landmap.title: Land, water and settlement
landmap.body: Pixels darker than −15 dB are water or bare sand; the threshold was checked against Sentinel-2 vegetation. Settlements are picked out by persistently bright radar returns.

banks.title: Banklines
banks.body: The west and east edges of the main river corridor are traced for every dry season, giving twelve positions of each bank.

erosion.title: Erosion per monsoon
erosion.body: Land in one dry season that is river or sand in the next. Patches under 1 ha, or not touching the channel, are dropped as noise.

sections.title: 500 m bank sections
sections.body: Each bank is cut into 500 m sections. For each section and year: past erosion and retreat, how the bank sits in the river, and long-term water history.

model.title: Model and ranking
model.body: A gradient-boosting model learns which sections lose at least 5 ha in a monsoon. Its output ranks the sections of each reach for the 2026 monsoon.

meaning.title: What the forecast means
meaning.body1: The model is trained to recognise sections that lose at least {{ha}} ha within the section's window in one monsoon. A section is {{len}} m of one bank; the exposure figures use the 2 km of land behind it.
meaning.body2: High, Medium and Low are relative: the top 10%, the next 20% and the remaining 70% of sections in each reach. They are not probabilities, and Low does not mean safe.

past.title: How well it worked on past years
past.body: To test it honestly, a model was trained only on monsoons up to {{last}} and then asked to rank the sections for {{from}}–{{to}}, which it had never seen. {{events}} of {{rows}} section-years had major erosion.
past.caption: Each year the riskiest 20% of sections in each reach are flagged. The highlighted rows are this model and the main baseline.
past.reading: Flagging the top 20%, the model caught {{gbm}} of the major-erosion events; repeating last year's erosion caught {{pers}}, a random pick {{rand}}. The margin over persistence is small (PR-AUC {{gbmAuc}} vs {{persAuc}}): past erosion is already a strong signal, and the model adds a modest amount on top.
past.metricsHelp: What PR-AUC, recall and precision mean
past.metricsHelpBody: Recall is the share of real major-erosion events that the flagged 20% caught. Precision is the share of flagged sections that really had major erosion. PR-AUC summarises the ranking across every possible cut; a random ranking scores about the share of events (here ≈ 0.13).

regions.title: Does it work in the other reach?
regions.body: Trained on Sirajganj and tested on Gaibandha, the model beats persistence. Trained on the smaller Gaibandha set and tested on Sirajganj, it does not. The final model uses both reaches.
regions.direction: Trained on the {{train}}, tested on the {{test}}

nisar.title: Early check with NISAR, 2026
nisar.body: The 2026 forecast was made before the monsoon. {{n}} NISAR passes up to {{date}} show where land has turned to water so far, so the forecast can be scored on a year and a sensor it never saw.
nisar.caption: {{events}} of {{n}} sections had major change so far. Top 20% flagged per reach.
nisar.shares: Sections the model called High had major change {{high}} of the time so far, against {{medium}} for Medium and {{low}} for Low. Persistence still has the higher recall this year.
nisar.alignment: These recall and precision figures use the top 20% of sections per reach. The map's High class is the top 10%. They are reported separately on purpose; one should not be read as the other.

drivers.title: What the model pays attention to
drivers.body: How much the model's PR-AUC drops when one input is shuffled, on the 2023–2025 test years. Longer bars mean the model leans on that input more.
drivers.caution: This is association inside the model across all sections. It is not proof of cause, and it does not explain the rank of any single section.

priority.title: How union priority is calculated
priority.body: Union priority combines the model's ranking with recent bank retreat and who lives nearby, so that it points to where attention matters most, not only where erosion is likeliest.
priority.levels: Levels: High at 0.70 or above, Medium at 0.50 or above, otherwise Low. Ranks are shown within each reach only.

bankline.def: The bank position from radar observations between November 2019 and April 2020.

monsoon.def: Land in the 2020 dry-season map that is river or sand in the 2021 map: the change across the 2020 monsoon.

forecastSeason.def: The monsoon the model ranks sections for, using data up to the 2026 dry season.

nisarObs.def: One radar pass on its actual acquisition date, every 12 days when available.

section.def: 500 m of one bank (west or east). Its exposure zone is the 2 km of land behind it.

exposure.def: People (WorldPop 2020) and buildings (Open Buildings v3) in the 2 km zone today. Context, not losses.

limits.title: Limitations
limits.years: Eleven monsoons of history; a rare extreme year may behave unlike any of them.
limits.relative: Classes are relative within each reach. A Low section in a very active reach can still lose land.
limits.settlement: Settlements are inferred from radar brightness, which misses some homes and includes some bright non-buildings.
limits.exposure: Population is a 2020 estimate and buildings a single snapshot; neither is a count of losses.
limits.weights: Priority weights are design choices, not measured effects.
limits.nisar: NISAR results are provisional until the falling-river passes of October and November are processed.
limits.coverage: Only two reaches of the Jamuna are covered, not the whole of either district.

about.title: About <hl>River Watch</hl>
about.lede: A hackathon prototype that explains a working erosion pipeline: what it measures, what it ranks, and how far its results can be trusted.

what.title: What this is
what.body1: River Watch shows the results of an offline Python pipeline that maps the Jamuna's banks from radar every year, measures erosion between years, and ranks riverbank sections for the coming monsoon.
what.body2: It is a static snapshot, not a live service and not an official warning system. Notices on this site are demonstrations of how a union-level advisory could look.

coverage.title: Coverage and dates
coverage.body: Two reaches of the Jamuna, defined by the study boxes below. Union boundaries come from geoBoundaries.
